source.title_on_document: Generative AI-Supported Creative Writing Among Primary School Students: A Study of Creative Writing Performance, Writing Self-Efficacy, and Flow State

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Its 'supplementary exploratory analysis' (Section 4.4, Table 4) is part of the main text.
supplement.holds: Nothing indicated. All reported statistics (Tables 1 to 4) are in the main text; no standard errors or regression output are reported anywhere.

paper_design_summary: Seventy-eight fifth-grade students from three classes of one primary school in eastern China were randomly assigned to write a roughly 300-word creative essay ('Design Future Cars', 25 minutes) with the chatbot Deepseek (n = 20), with a peer (n = 38, 19 pairs), or alone (n = 20); one week earlier all students wrote a similar essay alone as a pretest. Three researchers scored the handwritten essays on a 100-point rubric (originality 40, flexibility 30, elaboration 30), and students also completed self-report flow and writing self-efficacy scales.

studies.label: Classroom experiment: GenAI-supported vs peer-collaborative vs individual creative writing (fifth graders)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing condition for the week-2 essay: GenAI-supported writing (Deepseek), peer-collaborative writing (pairs), or individual writing
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions: (1) GenAI- supported writing group ( n = 20), in which students used GenAI to support the creativewriting task; (2) peer- collaborative writing group ( n = 38; 19 pairs)

arms.name: GenAI-supported writing group
arms.description: Students used Deepseek on computers as a 'thinking partner' while writing, after a specialized tutorial; task-sheet rules asked them to evaluate suggestions and avoid verbatim copying; final essay written by hand

arms.name: Peer-collaborative writing group
arms.description: Students paired (19 pairs) to collaboratively complete the creative writing task, no AI

arms.name: Individual writing group
arms.description: Students completed the creative writing task alone, no AI

participants.exclusions: None reported. 'No students or parents declined to participate after the formal consent process' (p. 4); Table 1 Ns (20, 38, 20) equal the assignment counts.
participants.who: Fifth-grade students aged 10-12 (M = 11, SD = 0.51), 42 boys and 36 girls, from three classes taught by the same teacher, recruited by convenience sampling; all already familiar with GenAI tools
participants.quote: A total of 78 students (aged 10–12 years; M = 11, SD = 0.51) from three classes were invited to participate in the study.

ai_tool.how_used: Multi-turn chat on computers during the 25-minute writing task; students prompted it mainly for idea generation (27 of 50 episodes) and idea elaboration (10 of 50), then wrote the final essay by hand (p. 5; p. 8, Table 4)

task.description: Essay of about 300 words, 'Design Future Cars' (week 2, treatment session); pretest 'Design Future Shoes' (week 1, all students alone). The authors note the task leaned toward expository and informational writing (p. 10).
task.duration: 25 minutes per essay; experiment lasted 2 weeks

outcomes.name: Creative writing performance score (week-2 essay)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three researchers ('three raters') scored each essay on a 100-point rubric: originality 40, flexibility 30, elaboration 30; only the total is reported. Week-2 Kendall's W = 0.89; consensus scores after discussion were used in analysis (p. 6, Section 3.4). Rater blinding to condition not stated. Peer-group scores are reported for 38 students although pairs wrote collaboratively; the paper does not say whether each pair's essay score was assigned to both members.

contrasts.reported: GenAI-supported 88.850 (SD 1.420, N = 20) vs individual 85.133 (SD 2.120, N = 20); omnibus one-way ANOVA across three groups F = 13.095, p = 0.000***, partial eta2 = 0.259, Cohen's f = 0.591; LSD post hoc a > c
GenAI-supported 88.850 (SD 1.420, N = 20) vs peer-collaborative 86.825 (SD 2.719, N = 38); omnibus one-way ANOVA F = 13.095, p = 0.000***, partial eta2 = 0.259, Cohen's f = 0.591; LSD post hoc a > b

data_and_code.data_url: Not posted; 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request' (p. 11, Data Availability Statement)

eligibility.reason: The paper states that 78 students were randomly assigned to GenAI-supported, peer-collaborative, or individual writing (p. 4, Section 3.1), and researchers scored creativity on the essays with a rubric (p. 6; p. 7, Table 1). 78 people across all arms meets the 50-person rule, though the GenAI vs individual contrast holds only 40 people. Caveats: the randomization procedure and unit are not described (students came from three intact classes, and arm sizes 20/38/20 are unequal), rater blinding is not stated, and flow and self-efficacy are self-reports that do not count as outcomes.

one_line_finding: Fifth graders writing with Deepseek scored 88.85 (SD 1.42, n = 20) on a 100-point creative writing rubric, versus 86.83 (SD 2.72, n = 38) for peer pairs and 85.13 (SD 2.12, n = 20) for individual writers (ANOVA F = 13.10, p < 0.001; LSD GenAI > both), p. 7, Table 1.
open_questions: How was random assignment carried out across the three classes? Could conditions coincide with classes? The paper says only 'randomly assigned' (p. 4).
In the peer group, did each of the 19 pairs write one essay whose score was given to both students (N = 38 in Table 1), or did each student write an essay? This affects the unit of analysis.
Were raters blind to condition? Not stated.
Only arm-level means and SDs and an omnibus F are reported; no pairwise mean differences, SEs, or pairwise p-values for the LSD comparisons.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports: writing self-efficacy (6-point scale; GenAI 5.276 SD 0.342, peer 5.022 SD 0.756, individual 4.812 SD 0.708; Welch F = 4.106, p = 0.023; p. 7, Table 2) and flow state (5-point scale; GenAI 3.919 SD 0.441, peer 4.428 SD 0.540, individual 4.031 SD 0.635; F = 6.974, p = 0.002; p. 8, Table 3). The week-1 pretest essay was written alone by all students before treatment (F = 2.56, p > 0.05 across groups; p. 4) and is a baseline, not an after_ai outcome; no post-AI unaided writing was measured. Table 4 (p. 8) codes 50 student-AI interaction episodes descriptively. The authors state the GenAI-group scores reflect AI-supported products, not unaided ability (p. 8).
